headline: From ‘Stranger Things’ to Broadway, Everyone Knows Joe Keery

paragraphs.text: Joe Keery reached high to grab a package of nori for a woman standing nearby.
“Should I get one of these?” he asked her sweetly. “Are they good?” He took another package for himself.

On the first Tuesday in November, Keery, 34, a star of the Netflix fantasia “Stranger Things” and a chart-topping solo musical artist, had blocked out the afternoon for errands. On the agenda: a frame shop, a florist’s for soil and a tiny houseplant, a Japanese grocery for mochi rice, part of a resolution to cook more. (A bandage covered a recent zucchini-related burn.) Then he would walk the 30-odd blocks to the Hudson Theater, where he is starring in a revival of the Jon Robin Baitz play “Other Desert Cities.”

That afternoon, Keery, who has an apartment nearby, had dressed casually in dark jeans, a denim jacket and a red-and-blue baseball cap, matching the “I Voted” sticker pasted to his shirt. It wasn’t the most camera-ready look. That didn’t deter the half-dozen fans who stopped Keery for selfies or several paparazzi. The woman in the grocery was the rare person who seemed not to recognize him.

Keery was gracious throughout, effortlessly decent. If there were Geiger counters to measure kindness, they would go crazy around him. He posed when asked and made time for a couple of student journalists outside a polling site. Asked about voting, he told them, “It’s invigorating and exciting to do and it makes you feel like you’re taking an actively participating role as a citizen.” At the frame shop, where he is a regular, he gave the owners his personal phone number, so that he could arrange discount Broadway tickets for them. I followed the man into traffic and didn’t think twice.
“Everyone who meets him falls in love with him,” Matt Duffer, a co-creator of “Stranger Things,” said.

Keery is ambivalent about this adulation. On his most recent album, “The Crux,” a song includes the lyrics: “I don’t want your money / I don’t care for fame / I don’t want to live a life where that’s my big exchange.”

So it’s a paradox that just about everyone thinks they know and love Keery, just at the moment when he is trying to complicate how people perceive him as an artist. That complication is why he put himself on Broadway, despite not having done a play since college.
“I really wanted to do something that felt like getting back to why I started doing this in the first place,” he said.

Keery has the problem and the gift of being associated with a single role, one he played for about a decade. He was 23 when he was cast in “Stranger Things” as Steve Harrington, a high school bully with unusually good hair. Matt and Ross Duffer, the creators of the series, watched plenty of audition tapes. Only Keery’s lofted Steve beyond stereotype. “He brought a humanity to him, a charisma,” Ross Duffer said in a recent interview.

Steve was meant to die at the end of the first season. Instead he survived, becoming a hero. He also became a lot more like Keery. “Joe’s charm was undeniable,” Matt Duffer said. “We just started to really lean into that.”

In between the show’s five seasons, many of his co-stars took on other jobs, diversifying their résumés. Keery didn’t do much. “Truly not for lack of trying,” he said. He wasn’t interested in roles that too closely resembled Steve, and casting directors turned him down for others. “Just because you have this thing on a silver platter doesn’t mean you get everything else,” he said.

Still, he kept making music, psychedelic synth pop that unpacked personal experience. A musician since his college days in Chicago, he’d had to part from an early band, Post Animal, when “Stranger Things” first aired. (Filming interfered with touring and fans started showing up to gigs in “Stranger Things” merch, which messed with the vibes.) But as a solo artist, who performs and records under the name Djo, he could make his own schedule. One bittersweet song, “End of Beginning,” which seems to reference his life before and after fame, has reached the top of several global charts.
As we sat, post-errands, in Union Square Park, a man stopped to tell Keery that he had his latest album on vinyl. “Oh, thank you, man,” Keery said. “Thank you. Thank you so much. Enjoy the day.”

As “Stranger Things” neared its final season, Keery made moves. He reunited with Post Animal. He starred in a season of “Fargo” and made a couple of movies. And he began looking for a play to appear in, as a way to reconnect with the actor and the person he had been before he was famous. He struggles to remember how people treated him back then, how he felt in his own skin. “Which is a little scary for me,” he said. “But I try not to get negative about it. Otherwise, I feel like it could be easy to spiral or feel trapped.”

He hadn’t heard of “Other Desert Cities,” a 2010 drama, set in 2004, that drops in on a prominent California family as they celebrate a fraught Christmas in Palm Springs. But he was invited to participate in a workshop of it last winter, opposite Allison Janney and Julia Louis-Dreyfus, and he found that he loved it. John Benjamin Hickey, the play’s director, loved him, too. “Joe was just so remarkably self-possessed and took such ownership of the part that it was sort of a no-brainer,” he said.

Rehearsing the play this summer and fall was daunting, especially as tour dates necessitated that he start a week late, but he enjoyed the luxury of working a scene again and again, going deeper each time. And thinking about what makes and breaks a family — he remains close to his parents and four sisters — was a pleasure, too.

Keery plays Trip, the family’s youngest child. Helen Shaw, in The New York Times, wrote that Keery, “a real discovery, manages to be droll with a heart.” For most of the play, Trip serves as a joker, a peacemaker. But in the second act, he delivers a monologue that concludes with the lines, “I am California! And California is not happy!” It’s a big, emotive speech. He delivers it with the naturalness and grace of someone who has been onstage all his life.

“Joe brings such ease,” said Lily Rabe, who plays his older sister in the play. She noted that Keery, who has the dressing room next to hers, was easy offstage, too: “He just does not carry himself at all like someone whose first job rocketed him to lightning-strike superstardom or someone who has women waiting in droves for him at the stage door.” (Several of Keery’s “Stranger Things” co-stars, including Charlie Heaton and Maya Hawke, have also come to see the show.)

Keery has never chased superstardom. He doesn’t want to seem ungrateful, and he isn’t. But he would live less publicly if he could. He seemed most joyful at the Japanese grocery, sincerely congratulating a new cashier on his first day on the job. “And on voting day, too!” he said. His face lit up when he talked about his family, about making music, about finding roles that show he is more than his charisma and wavy hair.
“I can surprise people a little bit,” he said. “Attractive to me in any piece of art is something that is shocking or subverts my expectation. I’m looking for ways to be able to do that.”
